title: Blue Penny Museum
about_landmark_text: This museum on the Caudan Waterfront, open since November 2001 and dedicated to Mauritian history and art, holds two of the rarest stamps on Earth: the 1847 "Post Office" stamps - a one-penny orange-red and two-pence blue modelled on Britain's Penny Black and bearing Queen Victoria's profile.
about_subject_text:
This room's maps trace Mauritius through five centuries of chartmaking - the story is older. Arab sailors crossing the Indian Ocean are thought to have sighted the island by the 10th century without ever settling it, logging it only as a trade-route marker: Dina Arobi - a name still visible decades later on Portuguese charts like the 1502 Cantino planisphere, which labelled the Mascarene islands by their old Arabic names before any European had landed. The name that stuck arrived on 20 September 1598: Admiral Wybrand van Warwyck's Dutch fleet, sheltering from a storm in a bay on the island's south-east coast - what's now Grand Port, not Port Louis - named it Port de Warwick after himself and renamed the whole island Prins Maurits van Nassau-eiland, honouring stadtholder Maurice of Nassau and, coincidentally, his own flagship, which shared the same name: the Mauritius. Only that second half survived three centuries of French and British rule after.

The colony fared worse than its name. A fitful century of settlement drowned one governor on a coastal survey in 1672 and drove another to quit in 1657; no gold or spice ever turned up, only ebony logged out within decades, while cyclones, drought, rats and sick cattle finished off the rest. By 1710 the Dutch East India Company withdrew its last governor, Abraham Momber van de Velde, leaving the island empty for five years until the French arrived. Only the rats and pigs they left behind endured - long enough to help hunt the fearless, nowhere-else-found dodo to extinction before the Dutch even packed up.

None of it marked Port Louis itself: the capital's history starts only with the French in 1715, five years into an empty island, and even the Dutch had landed on the coast's far side. These maps and ship models - Dina Arobi to Nassau-eiland to Mauritius - are the closest the city comes to remembering any of it.
interesting_fact: A consortium of Mauritian companies, led by the Mauritius Commercial Bank, paid $2,000,000 in 1993 just to bring the stamps home after almost 150 years abroad. To protect them from light damage, the real stamps are only illuminated for ten minutes on the quarter-past of every opening hour - the rest of the time, what you're looking at is a facsimile.

title: Port Louis Casino
clue_text: head roughly eastwards for about 150–200m - you are looking for a ship
puzzle_question: How many claws at the front of the ship?
puzzle_explanation: The casino's facade is built to resemble the bow of a pirate ship, complete with a bowsprit mast and figurehead-style statuary - the claws are part of that theatrical, ship-themed design.
about_landmark_text: This casino at Caudan Waterfront is part of the complex that opened on 25 November 1996, on land once occupied by warehouses and a meteorological observatory. It occupies the Barkly Wharf building, named for Sir Henry Barkly, Governor of Mauritius from 1863 to 1870, and is known for a striking facade styled like the bow of a pirate ship, complete with bowsprit mast and statuary.
interesting_fact: The building's pirate-ship facade - a bowsprit mast and figurehead-style statues built into the architecture - makes it one of the more theatrical pieces of commercial design on the whole waterfront, and it backs it up with scale: it's the largest casino in Port Louis, running 214 gaming machines and 16 table games under that pirate-ship roof.

title: SAJ Statue
clue_text: head along the waterfront - you are looking for a statue
puzzle_question: The taller of the 2 PM statues, what year was he born?
puzzle_explanation: Sir Anerood Jugnauth - "SAJ" - was born on 29 March 1930. He went on to serve as Prime Minister across three separate spells between 1982 and 2017, and as President from 2003 to 2012.
about_landmark_text: This bronze statue of Sir Anerood Jugnauth ("SAJ") was unveiled at the Port Louis Waterfront on 15 June 2024, honouring the former Prime Minister and President who dominated Mauritian politics for decades. It stands beside an earlier statue of Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, placing two of independent Mauritius's most prominent leaders side by side on the same esplanade.
interesting_fact: At 3.6 metres tall, the SAJ statue was built about 30 centimetres taller than the neighbouring Ramgoolam statue, and its Rs 13.5 million cost and sculptor Devanand Bungshee's likeness both drew public criticism at the time of unveiling.

title: Aapravasi Ghat World Heritage Site
clue_text: keep going in the same direction for about 350m - you are looking for a museum
puzzle_question: What year was this place made a World Heritage site?
puzzle_explanation: Aapravasi Ghat was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2006, recognised as the place where the "great experiment" of indentured labour began - almost half a million labourers passed through this depot between 1849 and 1923.
about_landmark_text: You're standing at the place where the modern indentured-labour diaspora began - though the practice itself predates this exact building. The first 36 indentured labourers reached Mauritius on 2 November 1834 aboard the ship Atlas, which had left India that September; they landed near the old Customs House, just metres from where you're standing now, fifteen years before this purpose-built depot even existed. Built in 1849, the Aapravasi Ghat - literally the 'Immigration Depot' - became the main entry point for almost 500,000 indentured labourers brought to Mauritius between 1849 and 1923, mostly from India but also China, Africa, Madagascar and Southeast Asia, to work the island's sugar plantations after the abolition of slavery. New arrivals bathed after weeks at sea, were medically inspected and vaccinated against smallpox, had their contracts read aloud in their own language, and usually spent about two days here completing the paperwork before being sent out to sugar estates across the island. It's been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006. Entry to the site and its Interpretation Centre is free.
interesting_fact: Roughly 70% of Mauritians today are descended from these indentured labourers - making this small 1,640 m² depot one of the most significant sites anywhere for understanding the roots of modern Mauritian society, and one of the earliest examples of a labour-migration system that would go on to reshape economies worldwide.

title: China Town South Gate
clue_text: next a short walk of about 130m - head back down Royal Road towards the south-west - you are looking for a gate
puzzle_question: Which city gifted the gate to Port Louis? - hint - you may need to translate
puzzle_explanation: This is one of Chinatown's ornamental Friendship Gates, a gift from Foshan in Guangdong province - Port Louis's twin city in China.
about_landmark_text: This is one of the ornamental Friendship Gates marking the entrance to Port Louis's Chinatown on Royal Road, one of the oldest Chinatowns in Africa. The gates symbolise the long-standing friendship between Mauritius and China. The first Chinese to reach the island didn't come by choice: in 1760 the French admiral Comte d'Estaing shipped around 300 Chinese men and their families here from Bencoolen in Sumatra to work, but they refused to labour under the conditions they found and were sent back. The community that stayed arrived in the 1780s, when more than 3,000 voluntary migrants sailed from Guangzhou on British, French and Danish ships. They were genuine tradespeople and traders, including blacksmiths, carpenters, cobblers and tailors, and they quickly founded a small Chinatown here, the Camp des Chinois, the forerunner of the quarter you're standing in. From Port Louis they spread fast: by the 1860s Chinese-run shops could be found all over the island.
interesting_fact: Chinese shopkeepers spread across Mauritius so quickly that in 1892 one colonial official wrote that however remote the corner of the island you found yourself in, a "boutique chinois" would already be there to meet you.

title: Manga Street Murals
address: Venpin Street, near Emmanuel Anquetil Street, Chinatown, Port Louis, Mauritius
clue_text: keep heading down Queen St then take a quick right and a left - you are looking for something artistic
puzzle_question: About half way along the street there is a sign for a "club" - what kind of club?
puzzle_explanation: Halfway along Venpin Street, in among the anime and manga-style murals painted by local artist Urmila Narsiah in 2020, hangs a sign for a fight club.
about_landmark_text: Bright anime eyes, mid-strike swordsmen and mist-wreathed heroines cover the shopfront shutters and walls along this narrow stretch of Venpin Street, near its corner with Emmanuel Anquetil Street - a lane Chinatown locals nicknamed "Manga Street" the moment the paint went up. Before 2020 it was just another derelict back alley behind Chinatown's main strip. The New Chinatown Foundation handed the walls over to volunteer artists that year to mark the 50th anniversary of diplomatic ties between Mauritius and China, and in a matter of weeks a forgotten passage became one of the most photographed corners of Port Louis.
interesting_fact: Mauritius's borders were shut for Covid when these murals went up in 2020, so there was no flying in an international street-art crew - the entire wall of Japanese manga and anime characters was painted almost single-handedly by one local artist, Urmila Narsiah.

title: Jummah Masjid
address: Royal Road, Queen St, Port Louis, Mauritius
clue_text: now you are heading inland - cross the road carefully and prepare for it to get noisy - turn left at Queen St - walk another block and start looking for a religious building
puzzle_question: How many segments do you see in the stained glass window above the door?
puzzle_explanation: The stained glass window above the Queen Street door is made up of nine segments.
about_landmark_text: Port Louis's principal mosque, the Jummah Masjid, fills the block between Royal Road and Queen Street in the heart of the old commercial quarter, and it has an entrance on each side. The main entrance faces Royal Road, beneath the mosque's name and its small green dome, while a second ornate gateway opens onto Queen Street. The city's mercantile community bought this plot in 1852 and consecrated the mosque a year later, when it went by a different name entirely - the "Mosque of the Arabs." What you're looking at today is largely a late-Victorian rebuild: a major expansion begun in 1878 under Jackaria Jan Mahomed dragged on for years, slowed by disease and building-supply shortages, and wasn't finished until 1895.
interesting_fact: The mosque blends Indian, Creole and Islamic architectural styles so seamlessly that it's often named one of the most beautiful religious buildings in Mauritius.

title: Central Market Port Louis
clue_text: next head west south west as the crow flies about 300m, but it is about 450 to walk - you are looking for a market
puzzle_question: What object sits above the main gate to the market?
puzzle_explanation: The market's wrought-iron main gate, dating from 1839, is topped with a clock - a small Victorian-era flourish on one of the city's best-loved pieces of period ironwork.
about_landmark_text: Step into the historic heart of Port Louis's daily life - a market that's been trading here, in one form or another, since 1828, moving to this site in 1833 and formally opening under British rule in 1839. Its wrought-iron gates, worked with floral motifs and dating from that same year, are one of the city's best-loved pieces of Victorian-era heritage; the building itself was heavily renovated between 2001 and 2004 after several fires, careful to keep its original character intact.
interesting_fact: For nearly two centuries this market has been where all of Mauritius's communities meet and trade side by side - Creole, Franco-Mauritian, Indian, Chinese and African - and locals still often call it the Bazaar or Victoria Market rather than by its official name. A serious fire tore through the market in 1996, badly damaging the building - the renovation that followed, running 2001 to 2004, was as much about repairing that fire damage as modernising a market that was already over 150 years old.

title: Statue of William Newton
clue_text: head to Place d'Armes - you are looking for a statue, but which one? This one shares a name with a scientist
puzzle_question: How many fingers does he have outstretched?
puzzle_explanation: Newton is shown with a single finger outstretched - a fitting pose for the barrister who spent thirty years leading the Reform Party's campaign for elected representation.
about_landmark_text: This statue honours Sir William Newton (1842-1915), a Mauritian lawyer of mixed Indo-Mauritian and Scottish descent who led the reformist movement launched in 1882 demanding an elected element in the colonial Legislative Council. His campaigning under the administration of Governor Sir John Pope Hennessy helped bring about the Constitutional Reform of 1885, which for the first time let Indo-Mauritians and other non-white islanders elect their own representatives.
interesting_fact: The Constitution Newton helped win came into force on 20 October 1885 - the first time in Mauritian history that non-white islanders could vote for their own representatives in the colonial legislature. Newton himself embodied the divide he fought to close: born in 1842 to an Indo-Mauritian mother and a Scottish father, he belonged to the island's "Gens de couleur" community that colonial law treated as second-class. He won a British scholarship to study law in England, came home to practise as a barrister, and led the Reform Party he founded for thirty years, right up until his death in 1915.

title: Mairie de Port Louis
address: 4 Bis Jules Koenig St, Port Louis, Mauritius
clue_text: next you are looking for a "hall" - walk southeast about 300m
puzzle_question: How many brown steps up to the front entrance?
puzzle_explanation: Twelve steps lead up to the front entrance of the city hall, built in 1965-66 to replace the old Hotel d'Europe that the council had bought in 1866 to serve as its town hall.
about_landmark_text: Port Louis's city hall stands here, seat of a municipal government with roots going back to 1790, when the Colonial Assembly created it during the French Revolution - the city's first mayor was a Mr Enouf. That early council didn't last; it was dissolved in 1820 and not reconstituted until 1850 under British rule, when Louis Lechelle became the town's first modern mayor, working out of a rented house before the council bought the old Hotel d'Europe in 1866 to serve as its town hall.
interesting_fact: The building you're looking at isn't that old colonial hotel - it replaced it. Construction started in 1965 and the new city hall was inaugurated in 1966, the same year Port Louis was formally upgraded from a 'Town' to a 'City.' The council itself is older than this building by 175 years and counting - first established in 1830 - and today it governs the city through eight electoral wards, 32 councillors, and a Lord Mayor elected by them.

title: Statue de Saint Louis
address: St. Louis Cathedral's Garden, Pope Hennessy St, Port Louis, Mauritius
clue_text: head down Jules Koenig St for about 150m - you are looking for another statue
puzzle_question: The name of what city is embossed onto the statue?
puzzle_explanation: Paris is embossed onto this statue of Louis IX of France - "Saint Louis", the only French king ever canonised, and the namesake of the cathedral behind him.
about_landmark_text: A bronze statue of Saint Louis - King Louis IX of France, the cathedral and city's namesake saint - stands on a stepped stone pedestal in the peaceful courtyard and garden directly outside Saint Louis Cathedral, on Pope Hennessy and Bourbon Streets. It shares the square with a separate 18th-century heritage obelisk that once served as a water fountain, together forming a quiet corner right at the cathedral's front doors.
interesting_fact: Louis IX is the only French king ever canonised a saint - he led two Crusades and died of dysentery outside Tunis in 1270. Mauritius's oldest cathedral, and the streets around this square, all carry his name because of that dedication.

title: Photographic Museum Of Mauritius
address: Rue du Vieux Conseil, Port Louis, Mauritius
clue_text: the next one is not so easy to find, retrace your steps a little and turn left into a back street, it is a museum with a NEGATIVE cryptic link?
puzzle_question: Next to the entrance there is a small plaque to commemorate a Ms Leblanc - what is her first name?
puzzle_explanation: The plaque beside the entrance commemorates Marie Leblanc. The museum itself was founded in 1966 by photographer Tristan Bréville and his wife, to preserve Mauritius's photographic record going back to 1839.
about_landmark_text: This museum of historic photography sits on Rue du Vieux Conseil, founded in 1966 by photographer Tristan Bréville and his wife to preserve the island's photographic memory going back to 1839. Housed in an 18th-century building that once belonged to French botanist and administrator Pierre Poivre, it holds over 50,000 old photographs of Mauritius, alongside a collection of historic cameras and equipment.
interesting_fact: Among its collection is one of the rarest lenses in photographic history, made by Charles Chevalier for Jacques Daguerre - inventor of the daguerreotype - in 1834, just a few years before photography itself was publicly unveiled.

title: Natural History Museum
clue_text: head for a museum where you can find a real dodo (or part of one) and other wonders of the scientific world
puzzle_question: To the nearest 10cm, how long was the egg of the great elephant bird of Madagascar said to measure?
puzzle_explanation: The extinct elephant bird of Madagascar laid the largest eggs of any known animal - around 30cm long, with the volume of more than 100 chicken eggs.
about_landmark_text: This is the Mauritius Institute's Natural History Museum, on the ground floor of a National Heritage building constructed between 1880 and 1884 and modelled partly on Sri Lanka's Colombo Museum. Its collections trace back to 1826, when naturalists Julien Desjardins and Louis Bouton first proposed a museum to the governor - the resulting Desjardins Museum opened in 1842, decades before the current building existed, and the institution was declared a National Museum in 2000. Entry to the museum is free.
interesting_fact: The museum's most complete dodo skeleton wasn't unearthed until 1904, discovered by a Port Louis barber named Étienne Thirioux, whose amateur fossil-hunting turned up two near-complete dodo skeletons - the finer one stayed here in Mauritius, the other ended up in a museum in Durban, South Africa. Remarkably, his discoveries went almost unrecognised by scientists for decades and were never properly described in scientific literature until long after his death.

title: Bust of Queen Victoria
address: Victoria Urban Terminal, Victoria Square, Port Louis, Mauritius
clue_text: next head west, about 550m as the crow flies, to the Port Louis transport urban terminal - you are looking for a lady you might have seen earlier on the walk
puzzle_question: In what year was the monument unveiled?
puzzle_explanation: When the bust first appeared in May 2023 it had no plaque at all - within days it was covered with a sheet, amid rumours it was being saved for King Charles III's coronation on 6 May 2023. The small plaque on its back now records the year it was finally unveiled.
about_landmark_text: Carved from stone, this bust of Queen Victoria stands inside the Victoria Urban Terminal - a Rs 1.9 billion transport and shopping hub built over the city's old Victoria station, which began life as a railway terminus before becoming Port Louis's busiest bus station. The first buses rolled in in March 2022, the restored colonial stone building at its heart was kept as part of the design, and a footbridge now links the terminal straight to the Metro Express. When the bust first appeared, commuters stopped to photograph the fine detail in the queen's crown and flower-worked robe, many assuming it must have been shipped in from abroad rather than carved by a local stonemason.
interesting_fact: When the bust first appeared it carried no plaque or inscription at all, leaving passers-by guessing who had carved it and why. Within days it vanished under a sheet - and word around the terminal was that it was being kept under wraps for a royal occasion in London.

title: Caudan Arts Centre
clue_text: last stop - you are heading for another theatre, which forms part of a centre - cross the tram line over a bridge to find it
puzzle_question: What shape is the main feature of the 3 storey mural that sits alongside the waterway, opposite Barkly Wharf?
puzzle_explanation: The Caudan Arts Centre opened in December 2018, the first new theatre built in Mauritius in nearly a century - completing this walk back at the Caudan Waterfront, where it all began.
about_landmark_text: This performing-arts venue at Caudan Waterfront was built on what was once a car park, inaugurated in December 2018 as the first new theatre built in Mauritius in nearly a century. Its 431-seat auditorium, designed by architect Maurice Giraud and Didier Ho Architecture with acoustics engineering by Arup, hosts drama, music and dance, alongside a restaurant, bars, a conference room and exhibition space.
interesting_fact: Before this venue opened in 2018, Mauritius had gone almost 100 years without a purpose-built theatre - making the Caudan Arts Centre the first new stage of its kind on the island in nearly a century.
